Messages.Author: nys...@cs.com
Messages.Body:
In my other thread ("A Better [?] Tournament Scoring System") I argued
that we no longer needed a victory point allocation system that is
structured to incentivize risk, since the game win system already
achieves this, and in a manner that completely eclipses any vp-related
incentive of the current system. For those who are unconvinced by
this argument, and feel that more still needs to be done to encourage
players to make progress towards ending games, I offer the following
alternate proposal:

1. Victory points are allocated as per the standard rules, except
that when a game is called for time, each player still in the game at
time out receives a full victory point.

3. A Game Win is given to the player with more victory points than
any other player, except that in a game called for time, a player with
less than 3 victory points cannot receive a game win. (In completed
games, it is still possible to win with 2 victory points, provided no
other player has 2 victory points).

4. Each player receives a "table score" for each game based on his
victory point total for each game. Each player with 1 victory point
for a game receives a "table score" of 0.2 for that game. Each player
with 2 victory points receives "table score" of 1.5 for that game.
Otherwise, one's "table score" for a game is identical to one's
victory points.

5. In determining tournament ranking, the total of one's victory
scores is used in place of total victory points (ie. is used to order
the ranking of those players with an equal number of game wins).

-----------------------------

Unlike the current VP allocation system, this proposal never has the
effect of altering the relative table ranking of players in a game.
Game winners are never created who would not have been winners under
the standard rules, nor under the standard rules paradigm; and people
who would be Game Winners under the standard rules are never denied
the game win here.

In tournaments, this system offers a "risk incentive" in preliminary
rounds to players who have not yet scored an oust, by giving them so
little to lose (minus 0.2 ts if ousted) versus what they have to gain
(plus 1.3 ts if they oust).

I have focussed the incentive at this level, since it is at this that
level that there is no immediate prospect of gaining or losing a game
win. Hence, it is only at this level that "table-score"
considerations are likely to influence player behavior.

It offers less of a table-score incentive to those who already have 1
oust (minus 1.3 if ousted versus plus 1.5 if they score a second
oust). But offering table-score incentives at this level would be
pointless, since at this stage, the lure of a game win will be a far
more powerful consideration. The Game Win one might earn from a
second oust is worth more than any table score.

Similarly, no effort is made here to offer further game finishing
incentives to a player who already has 2 ousts under his belt. This
could be done (by, for instance, making 4 vp worth a table score of 6
or more) but was avoided for two reasons: 1) the risk of losing the
game win would outweigh any table score bribe one could possibly
offer; and 2) continuing escalation of the table score unduly
increases the advantage of being seated at a 5-player table. Also, it
seems to me perfectly acceptable that a person with 2 ousts should
keep the game win provided only he can make it to time out. In
situations like this, it is his opponents, who under this proposal
have little to lose and much to gain, who have little to lose by any
desperate measures to sieze the leaders crown and finish the game on
their own terms.

"Table Splitting" becomes even less attractive than it already is
under the game win system. A 3/2 split is now a 3/1.5 split. A 5-way
tie grants 0.2 to each player (regardless of the method used for
obtaining it -- time out, withdrawals, or 5-way simultaneous ousts).

>

Because John is angling to make game wins gained by getting to two
ousts and just sitting (or, alternatively, just barely getting to
the second oust before time) equal in value to someone who was
last-man-standing with two ousts in a game that finished.

It's more promotion of slow decks as being the equal of fast decks.
It punishes slow decks for being slow less than the existing system,
which to me is a negative. The notion of giving time out survivors
less reward is sort of interesting but doesn't strike me as being
very important. In my experience, the thing that contributes to
time outs in order of priority is:

1) Unfortunate metagame issues which prevent any deck at the table
from being effective at attacking its particular prey. (This
includes unfortunate deck ordering factors. People can only play
the cards they draw.)

2) People arriving at the table with slow-developing decks - lots
of intercept, bloat, combat defense but no offense.

3) People not playing as aggressively as they could.

(Maybe I'm forgetting other factors. I think almost everything
can be described

#1 is the worst contributor but something that we can't control.
Bad random deck ordering by some of the player also contributes
in the same way/looks like the same thing.

#2 is something we can control and should, to the extent the scoring
system can, without warping it in other ways too badly.

#3 is kind of variable. But usually in the situations where someone
would care about the difference between .2 VP and .5 VP (the change
John is making), they really don't have any reasonable chance of
scoring an oust anyway so it doesn't matter. IMHO, rewarding people
more for arriving at the table with slow decks will make more of a
difference and that difference will tend to snowball, as players see
more advantages to the surviving/building-up strategy that they'll
decide _they_ need to adopt it as well in order to compete in the
endgame. Eventually, glaciers will move faster than VtES tournament
games.

OK, I admit it, that last sentence is hyperbole. But I don't think
the change is good.

Fred

The distinction between this effect being a "purpose" vs. simply being "one
of its features" is without substance, especially when you turn around and
defend its existance. And the issue is not whether an arbritary value
assigned to a behavior can be defended as 'rational' is likewise pointless.
It's an expression of desirability, not a logical argument. The question
is whether it's desirable or not.

And your statement about "contribution to ending the game" is fallacious
in the exact same sense that Jeff Kuta's was: causing ousts before a game
ends isn't the sole measure of contribution in resolving a game. There is
no such measure except for one thing: did the player play a game which
didn't resolve. That's why there's only one penalty for failing to resolve
a game and it's applied to all the players who survive a game to time.

Just counting ousts doesn't take into account whether a player played
aggressively and used speedy methods to oust or conservatively and used
slow methods. Using the former is desirable and the latter undesirable
towards insuring games end more often. An oust that required a lot of
turns and time and occurred just before time was called should not be
counted as equal to one that took 20 minutes and a small number of turns.
I'm not saying players shouldn't have their choice of which route to
take. But the current system does a nice job of marginally penalizing
slow and deliberate decks and thus encouraging faster player and more
resolution of games, all else being equal. It's a misrepresentation to
suggest simply encouraging ousts does anything in this regard.

> position with your situation - a Table Win and 3 points, and the
> 2VP has no TW and 1.5 points, vs the current TW and 3, vs no TW
> and 2, or 4/0.2 instead of 4/1.

Yes, but it will not effect their behavior. Let's look at each
example:

3/2 splits:

Let's start with the case of the player with 2 ousts (who will get the
full value of his 3 vp if he avoids getting ousted). Your criticism
(or observations) somehow implies I *should* do something to give him
an incentive to make risky forward moves. But what can I possibly
offer him to make it worth his while? If he gets ousted, he loses the
game win. What can I offer him to make up for that risk except ... an
extra game win, or better yet, two extra game wins. Are we going to
start handing out multiple game wins per game? Because that's all one
could possibly offer that would have any meaning.

My system accepts the inevitable, realises one cannot use victory
point incentives to bribe a player who has scored exactly 2 ousts, and
instead focusses on those it *can* bribe. In this case, the bribe is
offered to the two *other* players, both of whom have virtually
nothing to gain from the status quo (3.0, 0.2, 0.2). They are the
ones who are bribed into taking risks.

This can have one of two effects. Either their risky ventures will
pay off, and they will put so much pressure on the Leader that (on the
principle that the best defense is sometimes a good offense -- do unto
others before they can do unto you) he is forced to try to defeat his
enemies before they defeat him. Or else, their desperate efforts at
victory will only lay them so wide open to the Leader that he finds he
just cannot pass up the ousting opportunities that fall in his lap
(after all -- one more oust will make his victory entirely secure).

4/1 splits

In this case, the Leader has no fear of losing the game win -- he will
get it even if ousted. So now his risk calculation is exactly even --
he stands to get 1 point if he ousts, lose one 1 point if he gets
ousted.

I explained in my original post why granting incentives to the leader
would be bad. It would potentially make a victory at a 5-player
tables too valuable compared to a victory at a 4-player tables.

Nonetheless, my system does create incentives for conflict -- not by
offering them to the leader -- but by offering them to the other
player. As above, the leader has every reason to offer a deal, but
the other player has no reason to accept. What good to him is a
measley 0.2 points if he has *any* remote chance of getting 1.5
points? He might as well go out fighting, and that probably means
that either his gamble will pay off and he will score his first oust,
or that by his desperate risk taking strategies he he will turn
himself into an easy meal.

I am amused by the idea that you think we need to incentize risk
taking to prevent 4/1 time outs. Such games are as close to finished
as a game can possibly be without actually being finished. A game
winner has already been firmly and irrevocably determined. I think
the leader will virtually always want to put the icing on the cake and
go for the sweep -- but so what if he doesn't?

> That doesn't really seem to incentivize taking a risk for a sweep,
> because 5/0 is no better than now, if you can find a cosy deal
> that will help and a player who accepts that it's better than
> nothing.

Ah, but it takes 2 to tango. The leader has every reason to offer a
"cozy" 3.0, 0.2, 0.2 deal to his 2 remaining enemies, or a "cozy" 4.0,
0.2 deal to one remaining enemy -- but what possible reason would the
opponents have to accept? This "cozy" bed has only room for one. If
their position is truly hopeless, they might accept the deal -- yes --
but in that case, why is the offer being made?

A 3.0, 1.5 deal, to a single remaining enemy with 1 oust, is a little
more "cozy" -- except that, by refusing the "cozy" deal and going
forward, the tables can be entirely reversed. By accepting the deal,
player 2 avoids the risk of losing 1.3 points. By risking this 1.3
points (compared to time out), and going forward, he stands a chance
of getting (compared to time out) -- not merely the measly +1.5 points
which more than evenly balances balances what he is risking -- but
also a GAME WIN.

My system creates a situation where any deal that is good for one
player will be bad for the other. Hence, maximum aggression and
conflict will be the norm.

value to the withdrawal rule if its function were only to permit
doomed players to escape their doom. The general theme of the game is
eat or be eaten.

LSJ wrote:
> Which is contrary to the idea that "the VEKN might as well ban
> withdrawal". That point being the one I was addressing.

Incorporating your objection into my prior analysis, my analysis could
be revised as follows:

>From the perspective of the withdrawing player, withdrawal can serve 4
functions: (1) a collusive purpose, intended to give another player
an advantage; (2) defensive purpose; (3) acknowledging a 2-player
deadlock, thereby ending the game; (4) breaking a multiplayer
"deadlock" by permitting the "deadlocked" player to retire, therby
permitting a more dynamic game to continue thereafter among the
remaining players.

(1). Collusive withdrawal:

A collusive purpose is generally illegitimate; and in any event, is
not something we need a withdrawal rule to promote.

(2). Defensive withdrawal.

A defensive purpose is legitimate, provided a withdrawal rule exists
for other reasons. However, it is not a reason to have a withdrawal
rule. The theme of the game is eat or be eaten, and to the extent
that withdrawal allows escape from those alternatives, it undermines
the theme of the game (as well as making tie games -- as opposed to
clear winners -- more likely).

The withdrawal rule, therefore, cannot be justified by appealing to
its collusive function or its defensive function. That leaves only
its last two functions -- variants of the deadlock-ending function.
The purpose served by the deadlock-ending function are either to speed
up a stalled game (in a multiplayer context) or to bring it to an end
(in a two player context).

(3). Deadlock (2-player):

Deadlock in a 2-player context can be subject to a relatively simple
analysis (compared to multiplayer). In a 2-player context, the game
always ends upon withdrawal, and one's opponent (under the current
VEKN rules) always receives twice the vp award that the withdrawer
receives. Also, in a one-on-one dynamic it is usually easier and far
less time consuming to determine if a deadlock is truly
unbreakable. Hence, in this context, a player will always prefer
time out or agreed-upon stalemate to withdrawal -- unless, of course,
he wants to grant his enemy a collusive benefit; or unless he fears
ousting, in which case it is really a "defensive withdrawal" (see
above). Hence, 2 player deadlocks do not provide justification for
the withdrawal rule under VEKN rules. It's only legitimate use is
defensive withdrawal, which, though legitimate if one has a withdrawal
rule, is not a reason to have a withdrawal rule.

The situation most subject to the temptation of collusion is the one
where each of 2 players has a victory point and each knows that by
withdrawing he will grant the other a game win. Obviously, there is a
strong temptation in such circumstances to arrange a withdrawal
according to a "coin toss" type deal.

The closest thing to an exception to the above analysis is the
situation where the withdrawing player already has 2 vp, and therefore
knows that, by withdrawing, he will secure the game win. Of course,
he can also secure a game win by surviving until time out or by
agreeing upon a stalemate, so, once again, the only reason to do this
is because he fears ousting. Hence, again, this is a kind of a
defensive deadlock. The thing that makes it (almost) an exception is
that the value of firmly securing of a game win is so great that the
prospect of eventual ousting -- no matter how remote or unlikely --
will justify the players interest in withdrawal.

(4). Deadlock (Multiplayer).

By "multiplayer deadlock" I mean a situation where a predator has no
hope of ousting his prey, but is in no foreseeable danger of being
ousted by his current predator. This situation differs from 2-player
deadlock in that (a) due to the complexity of the situation,
uncertainties are increased many-fold -- making it harder to
distinguish between a defensive withdrawal and a deadlock-breaking
withdrawal, and (b) the extra benefit one grants to one's opponent is
not immediately received, and will not be received at all if the game
goes to time.

Hence, the uncertainties that drive the "exception" cited under 2-
player deadlock will be far more common here. The uncertainties mean
that there will be many situations where it woll be impossible to
fault the decision of a player who, having scored two ousts, decides
to secure his victory by a withdrawal.

However, the same principles still generally apply. The half-vp
discount makes it far less likely that the deadlocked player will
think withdrawing is worthwhile. The logical thing to do, if he is
truly deadlocked, is to stay in the game, so as to make sure the game
goes to time, thereby depriving his unworthy opponents of the "last
man standing" benefit he cannot sieze for himself. Unless his fear of
being ousted and losing a half-vp is sufficiently great (in which case
we are dealing with a withdrawal that is mainly defensive), he will
have no interest in promoting a more dynamic game among the remaining
players. Why would he want one of them to get that half vp for
finishing? Why would he want to increase the chance that one of them
will claim a game win?

So, if the prospect of being ousted is merely a remote possibility,
then the remote fear of losing that half victory point will tend to be
more than balanced by the fact that, by withdrawing, he is promoting a
more dynamic game, and thereby increasing the chance that one of his
fellow players will secure a game win. If his fear of being ousted is
not-so remote, then we are dealing with a withdrawal that is primarily
defensive.

So, the same conclusion still applies, if a little more tentatively
due to the inherent uncertainties. Any situation where a player's
withdrawal may break a deadlock and promote a dynamic game is precisly
a situation where it would probably be wiser for the player to stay in
the game; for such situations, by their very nature, give him the
opportunity to instead to slow down the game and prevent his enemies
from claiming a victory he cannot claim for himself. The clearest
exceptions to this rule will be those cases that are actually
defensive withdrawals

Again, the only players for whom it will be, generally speaking,
advisable to withdraw will be those who have already scored 2 ousts.
These are the only people claiming for themselves more than they grant
their opponents.

Apart from that, we are lead, more or less, to the same conclusion.
The VEKN might as well ban withdrawal, for the half vp granted under
the current rules does not adequately recompense a player in most
situations where he might have both the opportunity and the temptation
to withdraw, and where the withdrawal is not primarily a defensive
attempt to avoid imminent ousting, and where the withdrawal might in
fact promote a more dynamic game among the remaining players.
